front: A scenario asks you to 'analyse the strategic position' of a company. Which framework do you reach for first, and what two buckets must never be mixed?
back: SWOT for a quick internal/external snapshot. The hard rule: Strengths and Weaknesses are INTERNAL (things the company controls or owns); Opportunities and Threats are EXTERNAL (market, regulation, rivals). Mixing them up is one of the most penalised errors in Section B.

front: Why do candidates lose marks for putting 'rising fuel costs' under Weaknesses and 'strong brand' under Opportunities?
back: Because they confused the internal/external split: fuel costs are an external Threat, the brand an internal Strength. Examiners want each factor in the correct quadrant before any TOWS-style linking.

front: When would you choose PESTEL over Porter's Five Forces — and can they appear in the same answer?
back: Use PESTEL when the question is about the broad external environment (politics, economy, society, technology, environment, law). Use Five Forces when it's about industry structure and competitive pressure. They often appear together: PESTEL sets the scene, Five Forces zooms into the industry.

front: A new low-cost entrant appears in a market with high fixed costs and few suppliers. Which two Five Forces pressures are biting, and what do they do to margins?
back: Threat of new entrants (low-cost rival) and rivalry among existing competitors, plus supplier power where suppliers are few. Each squeezes margins from a different direction: entrants undercut price, rivalry forces spending, powerful suppliers raise input costs.

front: Where does 'safety certification of finished goods' belong in Porter's value chain — inbound logistics, operations, or outbound logistics? Why?
back: Operations — it is part of transforming inputs into the finished product, not storing inputs (inbound) or distributing outputs (outbound). Candidates repeatedly park it in outbound logistics because it happens 'after production', but sequence logic says it precedes dispatch.

front: Outline the steps of a value-chain analysis when asked which activities create competitive advantage.
back: 1) List the company's activities in process order. 2) Classify each as primary (inbound, operations, outbound, marketing & sales, service) or support (infrastructure, HR, technology, procurement). 3) Identify where value/cost is concentrated. 4) Link strong activities to the claimed advantage (cost leadership or differentiation). 5) Recommend reinforcing or outsourcing weak links.

front: You have the SWOT. How do you turn it into a TOWS-style recommendation instead of four disconnected lists?
back: Cross-match: SO — use Strengths to seize Opportunities; WO — fix Weaknesses to access Opportunities; ST — use Strengths to blunt Threats; WT — defend where Weaknesses meet Threats. Each recommendation should name the specific strength and the specific threat/opportunity it pairs with.

front: A candidate recommends 'switch to electric vehicles to beat rising fuel costs' for a company whose scenario mentions no EV capability. What is the examiner's objection?
back: The recommendation is generic and off-scenario: it uses no information given about THIS company. Examiners reward ideas built from the scenario's own strengths and resources — e.g. using its strong brand or distribution to counter the threat — not imported textbook slogans.

front: Name the nine blocks of the business model canvas — and in one line, what question does the whole canvas answer?
back: Customer segments, value propositions, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partnerships, cost structure. The canvas answers: how does the business create, deliver and capture value? If asked to 'describe the business model', structure the answer around these blocks.

front: A question offers three strategic options and asks for a recommendation. What is the mark-earning sequence?
back: 1) State evaluation criteria drawn from the scenario (cost, risk, fit with objectives, speed). 2) Evaluate EACH option against the criteria — never skip one. 3) Compare them explicitly. 4) Give one clear recommendation with reasons. Candidates who analyse only their favourite option forfeit the marks allocated to evaluating the others.

front: A candidate evaluates one of three options thoroughly, then recommends it. Why does this still lose marks?
back: The requirement was to evaluate the options (plural) before choosing. Thorough analysis of one option earns only its share; the unexamined options' marks are simply gone. 'Evaluate all, then decide' is a standing examiner expectation.

front: Distinguish efficiency from effectiveness — and give a one-line test for each.
back: Efficiency = doing things right: output per unit of input (cost per unit). Effectiveness = doing the right things: hitting the objective (market share target met?). A firm can be efficient yet ineffective — producing cheaply something nobody wants.

front: A scenario asks whether to make a component in-house or buy it. Which costs are relevant, and which common cost must be excluded?
back: Relevant: incremental costs that differ between the options — variable production cost, any extra fixed cost of making, the purchase price, plus opportunity cost of capacity used. Exclude: sunk costs (past spend) and allocated fixed overheads that continue either way.

front: How does a higher proportion of fixed costs change a company's risk profile when demand falls?
back: It raises operating leverage: with high fixed costs, a small fall in sales causes a disproportionately large fall in profit. So a fixed-cost-heavy business looks more profitable in good times but is riskier in downturns — relevant when evaluating expansion or automation options.

front: In an ethics case, a model asks you to judge an action on 'fairness' and 'rightness'. What does each lens actually test?
back: Fairness tests equitable treatment: who gains, who loses, and are affected parties (regulators, customers, patients) treated justly? Rightness tests alignment with duties, rules and principles — does the action comply with the law, codes and professional obligations? They are different lenses, not synonyms.

front: Fairness vs rightness: a manager hides a product defect to protect jobs at the factory. Which lens condemns it first?
back: Rightness: concealing a defect breaches duties to regulators and customers regardless of motive. Fairness then asks who bears the cost — patients or consumers exposed to risk. Candidates who treat the two words as interchangeable miss the separate marks each lens carries.

front: You have applied an ethics model to a case. What must the final paragraph do, and what happens if it doesn't?
back: It must give a clear overall recommendation — e.g. 'the non-compliance should be disclosed' — synthesising the analysis into a decision. A model evaluation that never becomes a decision reads as unfinished; examiners explicitly note the missing conclusion.

front: Why is 'not disclosing looks profitable because we avoid an immediate loss' a weak ethical analysis?
back: It judges profitability on a short-term horizon only. A proper analysis weighs long-term regulatory, reputational and business risks of concealment against the one-off saving — the time horizon must extend past the immediate outcome.

front: Define 'business model' in exam-usable language.
back: The logic by which a business creates value for customers, delivers it, and captures some of that value as profit — who it serves, what it offers, how it operates, and how it makes money.

front: A scenario mentions rising interest rates, new labour laws, and changing consumer tastes. Which PESTEL letters are these, and why does the classification matter?
back: Economic, Legal, Social. Classification matters because examiners allocate marks to spotting the right factor family; a misclassified factor (e.g. calling a law 'political') signals you don't understand the framework.

front: What makes a strategic recommendation 'generic' in the examiner's eyes, and how do you fix it?
back: Generic = it could apply to any company and uses none of the scenario's facts. Fix: anchor every recommendation in a named scenario strength, resource or constraint, and explain the mechanism — HOW this company's specific capability counters this specific issue.

front: When is break-even analysis the right tool in a managerial-analysis answer?
back: When the question turns on volume, pricing or cost-structure choices — e.g. whether a new product, price cut or automation pays off. Break-even = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit; it tells you the volume at which the decision stops losing money, not whether demand will reach it.

front: Contrast economies of scale with economies of scope — one line each, one example each.
back: Scale: unit cost falls as volume of the SAME product rises (a bigger factory). Scope: unit cost falls by producing DIFFERENT products together (shared distribution for two product lines).

front: Give a reliable structure for answering 'analyse the company's strategic position' in Section B.
back: 1) One-paragraph scene-set. 2) Apply the framework the requirement hints at (SWOT/PESTEL/Five Forces/value chain) — state which and why. 3) Work through the framework using ONLY scenario facts. 4) Synthesise: what does the analysis mean for the company's position? 5) If asked, recommend. Application to the scenario, not framework recitation, earns the marks.

front: Strategic vs operational decisions: how do you tell them apart in a scenario?
back: Strategic: long-term, hard to reverse, shape direction (enter a new market, outsource manufacturing). Operational: short-term, routine, implement strategy (rostering, reorder levels). The exam tests strategy — if your recommendation is purely operational, you've probably pitched at the wrong level.

front: Define business risk in a way that separates it from financial risk.
back: Business risk is the variability of operating profit from the firm's markets and operations (demand, competition, costs). Financial risk is the extra variability imposed on shareholders by debt — fixed finance costs that must be paid whatever operating profit is.

front: List the four standard responses to an identified risk, with a one-line example of each.
back: Avoid (exit the risky activity), Reduce (controls, diversification), Transfer (insurance, hedging, outsourcing), Accept (bear it, within appetite — with contingency). A complete risk answer names the response AND the residual risk left behind.

front: Outline the risk management process as a cycle.
back: Identify risks → assess likelihood and impact → decide responses (avoid/reduce/transfer/accept) → implement controls → monitor and review. It is a cycle because new risks emerge and old assessments decay — a one-off exercise is a common examiner criticism.

front: Risk appetite vs risk tolerance — what's the difference?
back: Appetite is the broad amount of risk the board is willing to take to achieve objectives (strategic, qualitative). Tolerance is the specific acceptable variation around an objective (quantitative bounds, e.g. 'FX losses within 2% of revenue'). Tolerance operationalises appetite.

front: An exporter expects USD 2m in three months and fears the rupee strengthening. Which option gives protection — a call or a put on USD — and why?
back: A put option on USD: it gives the right to SELL dollars at the agreed rate, which is exactly what an exporter receiving dollars needs. A call would give the right to buy — the importer's instrument. Choosing the wrong side is a classic examined error.

front: In an options-hedge answer, a candidate computes the payoff if the option is exercised but never considers not exercising. What's missing?
back: The required scenario comparison: an option's value includes the right to walk away. A complete analysis evaluates exercise vs non-exercise (lapse) and picks the better outcome — omitting the 'do not exercise' leg forfeits those marks.

front: A share price is quoted Rs 78 cum-dividend with a Rs 8 dividend just declared. What equity price goes into a valuation model, and why?
back: Rs 70 ex-dividend: the buyer of the share at cum-dividend price will not receive the declared dividend, so the dividend must be stripped out before applying models like Gordon's growth. Using Rs 78 overstates value — a specifically flagged examiner trap.

front: A 1-for-4 rights issue on 80m shares at Rs 10 nominal plus Rs 40 premium: how many new shares, and at what issue price?
back: 20 million new shares (80m ÷ 4) at Rs 50 each (Rs 10 nominal + Rs 40 premium). The trap is treating the Rs 40 premium as the whole price, or miscomputing the entitlement ratio.

front: When is a forward contract preferable to an options hedge for currency risk?
back: When the exposure is certain and the firm wants cost certainty: a forward locks the rate with no premium, but removes all upside. Options suit uncertain exposures or when management wants to keep favourable moves — at the cost of the premium.

front: Transaction vs translation vs economic FX exposure — one line each.
back: Transaction: gains/losses on contracted foreign-currency cash flows. Translation: accounting effect of consolidating foreign subsidiaries. Economic: long-term effect of exchange rates on competitiveness and future cash flows.

front: How does a money-market hedge work for a foreign-currency receipt?
back: Borrow in the foreign currency now (creating a liability that the receipt will settle), convert the borrowing to home currency at spot, and invest/use it. The receipt repays the loan — the exchange risk is replaced by the interest differential.

front: What is Value at Risk (VaR), in plain words?
back: The maximum expected loss over a set period at a given confidence level — e.g. 'one-day 95% VaR of Rs 5m' means losses should exceed Rs 5m on only about one day in twenty. It summarises risk in one number but says nothing about how bad the worst 5% gets.

front: How does gearing affect the cost of equity in the traditional view?
back: Higher gearing raises financial risk, so shareholders demand a higher return — cost of equity rises with the debt-equity ratio. (Under MM with tax, the WACC falls initially as cheap debt replaces equity, but the equity holders' required return still climbs.)

front: Name the components of the Gordon growth model and state its key assumption.
back: Value = D1 ÷ (Ke − g): next dividend, cost of equity, constant dividend growth. Key assumption: dividends grow at a constant rate forever and Ke exceeds g — it collapses for firms with unstable or supernormal growth.

front: What is leading and lagging in FX risk management, and when is each used?
back: Leading = paying early / collecting early; lagging = delaying. Used between group companies: lead payments in a weakening currency, lag them in a strengthening one. It only works where you control the timing — typically intra-group.

front: Systematic vs unsystematic risk — and which one can diversification remove?
back: Systematic (market) risk affects all firms — interest rates, recessions — and cannot be diversified away. Unsystematic (firm-specific) risk — a factory fire, a lost contract — can be reduced by diversification. Only systematic risk is rewarded with higher expected return.

front: What belongs in a risk register, and why do examiners like seeing one referenced?
back: Risk description, owner, likelihood, impact, response, residual risk, review date. It shows the full cycle — identification through monitoring — rather than a one-off list of risks with no ownership or follow-up.

front: Why do candidates lose marks for listing risks without analysing impact?
back: A risk list is identification only. Marks sit in assessment: how likely, how large the impact (quantified where possible), which objectives it threatens, and what the response is. 'Risk: exchange rates' with no impact analysis is half an answer.

front: How do interest-rate risk and a company's debt profile interact?
back: Floating-rate or short-term debt exposes the firm to rate rises (higher finance costs, lower interest cover); fixed long-term debt locks cost but forfeits falls. The hedge choice (e.g. interest-rate swap, FRA) follows from which side of that trade-off the firm sits on.

front: What is sensitivity analysis, and what is its main limitation?
back: Vary one key variable at a time (price, volume, cost) to find the break-even value or the NPV impact. Limitation: it ignores correlation between variables — in reality price and volume move together — which is why scenario analysis (coherent bundles of changes) complements it.

front: When appraising a project, the Rs 15m feasibility study is already spent. Include it or exclude it — and what goes wrong if you get this wrong?
back: Exclude it: it is a sunk cost, unrecoverable whatever the decision. Including it overstates the initial outflow and then corrupts every downstream figure — depreciation, residual value, disposal profit — because the error cascades.

front: Demand grows 12% a year but the plant caps at 9,000 units. A candidate projects Year 5 sales from demand alone. What is the error and its effect?
back: Ignoring the capacity cap: Year 5 sales must be capped at 9,000 units. Unconstrained projections overstate revenue, variable costs and contribution together — a single missed constraint corrupting the whole forecast.

front: Only 25% of sales are on credit. On what sales figure are trade receivables based?
back: Credit sales only. Basing receivables days on total sales overstates the balance — the working-capital answer must follow the scenario's stated credit proportion, not total revenue.

front: Fixed manufacturing overhead is Rs 574m base plus Rs 85m incremental after expansion. Why is 'Rs 2,050 × 390,000 units' wrong?
back: Because Rs 2,050 was a per-unit ALLOCATION of the old base, not a true variable rate. The correct fixed total is Rs 659m (574 + 85). Re-applying an old absorption rate at a new volume double-counts fixed cost — a specifically flagged error.

front: Import duty is payable immediately on arrival with no credit period. Does it sit inside trade payables with raw-material cost?
back: No: only costs enjoying a credit period belong in payables. Immediately-payable duty is a cash outflow at arrival. Keeping it inside payables overstates current liabilities and understates the early cash outflow.

front: Work-in-progress is 50% complete on conversion costs. How do you value it, and what do candidates get wrong?
back: Materials at 100% plus conversion costs at 50% of the stage cost. Errors: ignoring WIP entirely, or applying conversion at 100% — both overstate WIP and therefore overstate the working-capital requirement.

front: A sales-promotion expense has a 30-day payment period. It is an expense — so is it in trade payables?
back: Yes: anything with a genuine credit period is a current liability at the reporting date. Candidates who put only suppliers' invoices into payables understate working capital.

front: State the DuPont decomposition of ROE and what each leg tells you.
back: ROE = net margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier (profitability × efficiency × leverage). It shows whether high ROE comes from real operating performance or merely from leverage — the first question to ask of any 'impressive' ROE.

front: NPV vs IRR: when can they disagree on two mutually exclusive projects, and which do you trust?
back: They can disagree when projects differ in scale or timing (IRR is a rate, blind to size). Trust NPV: it measures absolute wealth created in today's money, consistent with shareholder wealth maximisation. IRR's reinvestment-at-IRR assumption is the theoretical weak point.

front: What makes a cash flow 'relevant' for investment appraisal?
back: It must be incremental (caused by the decision), future (not sunk), and cash (not accounting allocations like depreciation — though the tax shield on depreciation IS a cash flow). Financing flows are excluded when the discount rate already reflects the cost of capital.

front: What is the cash operating cycle, and which way should management want it to move?
back: Inventory days + receivables days − payables days: the time cash is tied up between paying suppliers and collecting from customers. Shorter is better — it means less working-capital funding — achieved by faster collection, leaner inventory, or negotiated longer supplier credit.

front: A company's current ratio is strong but its quick ratio is weak. What does that combination signal?
back: Liquidity depends heavily on inventory: strip inventory out and cover looks thin. It flags slow-moving or obsolete stock risk — the analyst should check inventory days and ageing before concluding the firm is liquid.

front: Gearing is rising while interest cover is falling. What story are the two ratios telling together?
back: The firm is taking on more debt AND finding it harder to service: financial risk is rising on both the balance-sheet and income-statement measures. Either ratio alone could mislead; together they confirm deteriorating debt capacity.

front: Payback vs discounted payback — what does discounting add?
back: Discounting adds the time value of money: discounted payback measures how long until cumulative DISCOUNTED cash flows cover the outlay. It is still a liquidity/risk measure, not a wealth measure — it ignores cash flows after payback, which NPV captures.

front: An investment question gives no explicit assumptions. What should your answer still contain?
back: Stated assumptions: list every judgment you made (inflation treatment, tax timing, working-capital basis, residual value). Examiners award marks for explicit, reasonable assumptions — a silent assumption that turns out wrong looks like an error; a stated one looks like judgment.

front: Give the mark-earning structure for a Section B investment-appraisal answer.
back: 1) State basis and assumptions. 2) Lay out workings year by year with clear labels and units. 3) Compute NPV (and IRR/sensitivity if asked). 4) Interpret: accept/reject with reference to the criterion. 5) Note non-financial factors and sensitivity. A correct NPV with no recommendation, or workings nobody can follow, leaks marks.

front: A candidate computes the NPV correctly but never states whether to accept the project. Where did the marks go?
back: To the missing conclusion and recommendation: appraisal is decision support, and the decision is part of the requirement. Examiners also expect the key sensitivities — which variable would flip the decision — not just a single NPV number.

front: Why can a profitable company still face a liquidity crisis?
back: Profit is not cash: profits tied up in receivables and inventory, heavy capital expenditure, or debt repayments can leave a profitable firm unable to pay its bills. This is exactly why working-capital and cash-flow analysis sit alongside ratio analysis.

front: Accounting profit vs cash flow in appraisal — why does the exam insist on cash?
back: Profit includes non-cash allocations (depreciation) and follows accrual timing; investment decisions depend on when cash actually moves, because discounting is time-sensitive. Appraisal therefore starts from cash flows, bringing depreciation back only via its tax shield.

front: How do you handle inflation consistently in an NPV computation?
back: Either nominal cash flows at the nominal discount rate, or real cash flows at the real rate — never mix. If the scenario gives current prices and a general inflation rate, inflate each year's flows (nominal approach) unless told otherwise, and say so.

front: A question asks you to identify sustainability matters in a scenario. What classification must follow the identification?
back: Each matter must be classified under one of the three ESG pillars — Environmental, Social, or Governance. Identification alone earns limited credit; the explicit classification was the requirement candidates skipped.

front: Candidates correctly concluded a company was greenwashing, but their justification mentioned only environmental failures. Why did this lose marks?
back: The three-pillar view collapsed into an environment-only argument: social and governance failures in the scenario went unmentioned. A greenwashing conclusion must be justified across all three pillars where the evidence exists.

front: What is greenwashing, in exam-usable language?
back: Presenting the company's sustainability performance as better than it is — selective disclosure, vague claims, or highlighting minor green initiatives while hiding material negative impacts. The exam tests spotting the gap between claims and evidence.

front: Name the three ESG pillars and give two example matters for each.
back: Environmental: carbon emissions, waste and water use. Social: labour practices, community impact, product safety. Governance: board independence, anti-corruption, executive pay. Keep examples scenario-linked in answers, not generic lists.

front: A requirement asks for recommendations to align a company with a recognised sustainability framework. What structure earns the marks?
back: 1) Identify the company's material sustainability gaps from the scenario. 2) Name a recognised framework relevant to those gaps. 3) Recommend specific actions mapped to the framework's areas. 4) Note expected benefits and implementation considerations. Candidates who saw the 'why it matters' but couldn't propose framework-aligned actions lost these marks.

front: What does 'materiality' mean in sustainability reporting?
back: A sustainability matter is material if omitting or misstating it could influence the decisions of the report's users — investors, lenders, regulators, the public. It is the filter that decides what belongs in the report, mirroring financial materiality but with a wider stakeholder set.

front: Triple bottom line vs ESG — are they the same idea?
back: Related but different lenses: the triple bottom line (people, planet, profit) is a performance philosophy — measure success on three dimensions. ESG is the investor-facing framework of Environmental, Social and Governance factors used to assess risk and opportunity. TBL is the 'why', ESG the structured 'what to look at'.

front: How can sustainability performance affect a company's cost of capital?
back: Poor ESG raises perceived risk — lenders price in regulatory fines, stranded assets or reputational shocks; strong ESG can widen the investor base and lower funding costs. The link runs through risk, which is why sustainability sits naturally in this paper's risk-management area.

front: What is the role of the ISSB / IFRS S1 baseline in sustainability reporting?
back: It provides a global baseline for disclosing sustainability-related financial information so investors can compare companies. In exam terms: know that S1 sets the general disclosure requirements and that material sustainability risks belong in investor-facing reporting, not just in a separate CSR narrative.

front: How should an answer distinguish a company's sustainability claims from its actual performance?
back: Test each claim against scenario evidence: disclosed metrics vs targets, third-party assurance, consistency across pillars, and whether negative matters are disclosed or buried. Unsupported claims flagged against contradictory evidence is the core greenwashing-detection skill.

front: What is the circular economy, in one exam-ready sentence?
back: An economic model that keeps products and materials in use — design out waste, reuse, repair, recycle — so growth decouples from virgin resource consumption; the exam contrasts it with the linear take-make-dispose model.

front: Why does listing 'carbon emissions, staff welfare, board diversity' without comment earn so little in a sustainability question?
back: Because it is identification without analysis: no pillar classification, no link to the company's specific circumstances, no assessment of materiality, and no recommendation. The examiner's ladder is identify → classify → assess → recommend — each rung carries marks.

front: What is the Knowledge Reference area for, and how should you use it in revision?
back: It is the indexed map of examinable technical knowledge (IFRS/IAS treatments, core definitions) that underpins application. Use it as a look-up spine: when a case question turns on revenue, leases or expected credit losses, the Reference tells you which standard governs before you apply it.

front: An answer is technically sound but aimed at the wrong requirement. What exam technique prevents this?
back: Reading the requirement twice and underlining the command words and the exact deliverable before writing anything. Examiners note that misdirected answers are often technically competent — the failure is targeting, not knowledge — so planning time is never wasted.

front: How should you plan a Section B answer before writing?
back: 1) Parse the requirement: what is asked, how many marks, which exhibits matter. 2) Choose the framework. 3) Jot the structure with mark allocation per part. 4) Write to the plan, addressing every part. Examiners explicitly call for better exam technique — planning and covering every part.

front: Why do examiners keep penalising missing units and labels in workings?
back: Because 'Rs 659' could be thousands or millions, and an unlabeled column forces the marker to guess your logic. Every working needs units (Rs m), column headings, and row labels — presentation is part of professional competence and carries marks.

front: Section A vs Section B of the CAF-7 paper — what is the skills split?
back: Section A (45–55 marks) mixes short MCQs with constructed short responses: breadth and speed. Section B is longer case questions: depth, application to scenarios, and structured written answers. Revise accordingly — flashcards and quick recall for A, framework application practice for B.

front: How does rote learning show up as a weakness in examiner reports, and what replaces it?
back: Reports repeatedly note weak application of theory: candidates recite definitions but cannot use them on a new scenario. The replacement is active application — every concept revised by using it on a mini-case, which is exactly what these flashcards' scenario prompts are built for.

front: How should you allocate the 3 hours 15 minutes across the paper?
back: Roughly 1.8 minutes per mark (195 minutes ÷ 100 marks, keeping the 15-minute reading time for planning). Set a per-question time budget from its marks and move on when it expires — unfinished high-mark questions cost more than polished low-mark ones.

front: A candidate writes a long, correct explanation of a framework the question never asked for. What is the examiner's verdict?
back: Technically competent but misdirected: knowledge of an unasked framework earns little because the marks sit in answering the requirement set. Always match the tool to the requirement — the examiner rewards the right framework applied, not the most framework recited.
